title: Asilla's behavior-analysis AI at about 40 Japanese stations and buildings may have prompted two suicide interventions
summary: Kyodo (1 Jun 2026) reports Asilla's camera-analysis system at about 40 stations and buildings alerted guards in two cases where people later said they meant to jump; the claims are the developer's.
account: The date is the Kyodo report's publication as carried by The Straits Times; the two interventions are undated. Tokyo-based Asilla's system assesses the likelihood that a person will jump by analyzing behavior on security-camera footage, such as pacing or lingering near a platform edge or rooftop, and alerts security guards and station staff, in some cases with loudspeaker warnings. In one case it detected a man loitering in a non-customer area of a commercial facility; a guard found him and he later said he had intended to kill himself by jumping. In another, a child lingering near an upper-floor railing was found to have been writing a suicide note. Asilla says it trained the system since 2022 with around 200 facilities on about seven million pieces of footage. All details come from the company via Kyodo; no operator, police or academic confirmation was fetched. OECD AIM records the case (2026-06-01-db16).
purpose: Detect behavior indicating suicide risk (and illness, immobility or violence) in security-camera footage and alert staff.
system: Asilla AI behavior-analysis system for security cameras
deployer: About 40 railway stations and commercial buildings in Japan (operators not named)
taxonomy_note: Two interventions are described only by the developer; whether either person would otherwise have jumped is unknowable, so protective response. OECD AIM labels it an 'AI incident' with a positive rationale.

ratings.reason: Two people in apparent crisis were reached by guards after alerts, per the developer; no independent account of either case.
No operator-reported outcome or false-alert data in the fetched sources.

ai_role.statement: The system's alert prompted the guard's approach in both described cases; the intervention and the person's later statement are human. The sole source chain is the developer speaking to Kyodo, so system accuracy, alert volume and the operators' views are undocumented.
